items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of the Prime Minister’s answer to the last supplementary
question, when he introduced the nature of  his relationship with Ian Fletcher, can he
enlighten the House as to whether he has ha d further contact with Mr Fletcher since
their school days, perhaps in London?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I cannot recall particular occasions; I am sure I may
well have done so. What I can say, if the member wants to know, is that my mother was
best friends with Ian Fletcher’s mother. If that makes a conspiracy, fair enough.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I move, That the House take note
of miscellaneous business . Yesterday Patrick Gower from TV3 said that the Prime
Minister “owned” Mr Shearer yesterday. We ll, today not only did we see him being
owned but also we saw Mr Grant Robert son being owned—owned over and over again.
Mr Robertson’s best theory now is that Mr Key’s mother  knew Mr Fletcher’s mother.
Well, golly gosh, I did not know that was against the law yet in New Zealand. But it is a
fantastic sort of indication of what they will  do. Poor old Mr Robertson! If you want to
know what Mr Robertson is really trying to  do, we just have a look at Eddie on The
Standard. It is a left -wing blog site that Trans Tasman talked about today, and what it
tells us is what is really going on in the La bour Party and why it is that Mr Shearer is
being set up day in, day out to ask the Prime Minister about whether or not he stands by
his statements. Why is it that he does not want  to talk about his st atements? Because he
has got bank statements—

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why doesn’t the member talk about  justice? Because she’s running
it down. She’s got nothing to say and she’s running it down.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: —and Mr Little is an angry little man—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! Would the me mber Andrew Little
lower the tone of his interjection, so that at least I can hear the member.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: Take a chill pill.
27 Mar 2013 General Debate 8987

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Mr Little really should take  the chill pill, should he not,
Dr Coleman? Having said that, we can see why Mr Little is angry. Of the three factions
in Labour, there is the right, which, apparently, is led by Mr Shearer or Mr Goff, and the
left, which is led by David Cunliffe, and we  have got the careeri st left, which Mr
Robertson leads. But where is Mr Little on the list? Mr Little is last on the left faction—
last on the left faction. Why would that be? Because Eddie, of course, is a woman, not a
man, working at the Amalgamated Engin eering, Printing and Manufacturing Union,
which, of course, is Mr Little’s union. So Mr  Little is actually be hind the factions. Mr
Little is getting louder and l ouder and angrier and angrier, and he might have to take
that little—calm down, have a nice bit of peppermint tea, and he might be all right.
So let us talk about what the country really cares about. It actually cares about us, the
Government, doing work with the people of New Zealand, with the marvellous Public
Service, which is working so well with the National-led Government and our coalition
colleagues. Have a look at law and order. Under Labour, what happened? Well, I do not
know. Four more prisons were built, crim e was up—what else did we have—and the
prison population was up from 5,000 to 8,000 in nearly 9 years. What is happening
under National? Four years of a Nationa l-led Government, and crime is down—
absolutely right down—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: 30,000 jobs gone.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: —and Mr Clark over there from somewhere in Dunedin
says that the jobs are down. Yes, they ar e in the prison service, and the reason, Mr
Clark, is that crime is down. Is that not a good thing? Anyway, what we are also seeing
is that crime is down, people are safer, prisone rs are being rehabilita ted, great work is
going on in the Department of Corrections, gr eat work is going on in the police, and
great work is going on in education and in ge tting people to actually learn to read and
write, not like Labour. Labour’s response to cr ime was always: “Let’s  talk really tough
about it and then do nothing. Lock them up. Don’t rehabilitate them.” The other policy
we got from Labour—the only one we got on law and order in the last 4 years—was
Charles Chauvel’s “Let’s get rid of three st rikes.” That is actually the only policy on
law and order that the Labour Party has not yet reneged on. So let us just see what
happens. The other day we saw Mr Shearer saying: “No, we’re not going to now have
no GST on fruit and vegetables. We’ve now re neged on Mr Cunliffe’s policy.” Let us
see what he does on Mr Chauvel’s policy.
But at the end of the day all people want for New Zealand is that we work for them.
The Labour Party is working for itself, w ith factions going ar ound factionalising. My
dear old friend Shane Jones—I think he is part of Mr Shearer’s faction at the moment. It
could change. It depends on how the votes ar e. Mr Shearer is doing a great job. I was
thinking of actually saying to Mr Shearer th at I could start up a “Citizens for Shearer”
campaign. It worked really well in 1975 for Mr Rowling. I am thi nking of starting it. I
will get 100 worthies, all of whom, obviousl y, are friends of the Labour Party, and we
will go and help Mr Shearer, because we want  him to stay. I am his biggest supporter. I
think he is a great man. He has no memory of the US$100,000—it is US$175,000, is it
not, as I recall now—in that New York bank account. That is the rumour I have heard,
and why not? It sounds like a good rumour to  me. But, actually, this is the poor man
who, day in, day out, is asking the Prime Minister about statements—can he remember
them? This is the man who cannot even remember US$175,000 in a bank account.
But, of course, he could al ways just show us the money—show us the money. Show
us the money, Mr Shearer. Why do you not just show us the money? And we will all see
how it is that he can forget  that. But this is the man whom the Labour Party at the
moment says it wants to lead the country. Well, we know what that means. It means
8988 General Debate 27 Mar 2013
Russel Norman as Minister of Finance, or  possibly Russel Norman as deputy leader,
even, of the country. And what will that mean? Utter oblivion for this country.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First) : Well, I think that is an
improvement on the last time, Mr Speaker. Pros titution is not illegal in New Zealand. I
know that, you know that, and the National Government should also know that. But that
does not mean that Government policies shou ld be aiding and abet ting the sex industry.
[Interruption] Oh, look at them now. They do not like it when they hear something that
their Government has failed to address. Alcohol is not illegal, either. It is not illegal,
either, but that industry is surrounded by a range  of laws and regulations to mitigate the
harm it does to society.
What the public wants is leadership, some  leadership—something that the National
Government has failed to deliv er. It wants leadership from the Government in the area
of prostitution, because the fact is that the se x industry creates a serious risk and danger
to society, as well as to those working dire ctly in the sex industry. Recently, we have
seen the Minister of Immigration having to advise international students not to enter the
sex industry. So he must know something—he  must know something in this area. On
the new Immigration New Zealand employment  advice website international students
are being warned against working in the sex in dustry. Sam Lotu-Iiga, you need to listen
to this because a lot of t hose people are probably living in the Maungakiekie area. The
question the public is asking is—

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. I am sorry, but I am
struggling to hear this member, with the volume in here. Could we check the sound
system, because I am really struggling with it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am having absolutely no problem hearing the member. It is
a very good speech. Would the member continue.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : Thank you, Mr Speaker. I am sure
that member has now learnt something important, for a change. The question the public
is asking is what took the Government so long. What took the Government so long to
act? Has the Government not b een monitoring these student s coming into this country
and engaging in this kind of work—the se x industry, that is? Perhaps the Government
finds sex work either not sexy enough, or too sexy—too sexy to deal with.
Since the introduction of the Prostitution Reform Act 2003 the issues with
prostitution have got worse. It is out of c ontrol in South Auckland and in Christchurch.
In South Auckland, for example, we have a ma jor issue in Papatoetoe, in Manurewa, in
Ōtāhuhu, and now recently in Ōtara, where 13-year-olds can earn something between
$500 and $600 a night. That is disgraceful. Where are the police?  Why are they not
monitoring these young girls?
The local residents, especially the elderly, have also been unfairly abused, unfairly
harassed, unfairly suppressed, and unfairly muzzled by these prostitutes. The law-
abiding residents of this country are too afraid  to ring the police. They are too afraid to
actually report to the local authorities, beca use they are too scared  of the intimidation
that they are receiving from these prostitutes. This is an  industry that has been given
$8.7 million—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How much?
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR: It has been given $8.7 million by the
Ministry of Health to get its act cleane d up. New Zealand First acknowledges, though,
that it is important that we support the in tention behind these f unds, especially around
the alcohol abuse, the drug abuse, the under-age  abuse, and, of course, the issues with
health-related matters. But have  we seen any reports? Has anyone received any reports
on whether there has been an improvement in  this area? I do not think we have. The
Minister of Health has not even presented us  with any reports to tell us how this $8.7
27 Mar 2013 General Debate 8989
million of taxpayers’ money has been spent by the New Zealand Prostitutes Collective.
There have been no updates.
Unfortunately, the problem of street prosti tution has got worse a nd is completely out
of control. By some reports, something like a third of the sex workers in Auckland are
Chinese. Is that not extraordinary? Is that  not extraordinary, Da vid Bennett? What is
going on here? How many of these people are recent migrants to New Zealand? How
many of them are also using student visas as  a front for a prostitution ring? Are they
able to properly reside and work in New Zealand? Prostitution is an issue, and I think
the Government should pull my bill out of th e ballot in order for this matter to be
resolved.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia
ora tātau katoa. Me waiho ake m ā taku Reo M āori e whakatau te puehu e rere haere nei
roto i t ēnei Whare i t ēnei w ā. Ia 5 tau ka t ū te tatauranga nui, me k ī, ko te census ki
runga i te mata o te whe nua—ia 5 tau. Whai muri, ko t ētahi kaupapa e k īia ana, ko te
Māori Option. Ka mutu, he aha te M āori Option e kōrerohia ana? Arā, ko tērā kia taea e
ngā mea Māori nei te haere mai i te general roll ki te M āori roll, i te M āori roll rānei ki
te general roll. Ko te mate k ē o t ēnei kaupapa e 4 marama noa iho te w āhi kua
whakatahangia kia taea e te M āori te whakawhiti mai, t ētahi taha ki t ētahi taha—4
marama noa iho. Ki te kore t ētahi M āori e whakawhiti, me k ī, kua noho k ōhatu tana
noho i runga i t ērā rārangi īngoa, tērā pea m ō ngā pōti e rua. N ō reira, he kaupapa nui
tērā ki ngā mea, ngā kaipōti Māori.
He hītori anō rā, he k ōrero o nehe t ō ngā tūru Māori. I te tau 1967, e wh ā ngā tūru
Māori—e whā ngā tūru Māori. Ā, ka mutu, i te tau 1996 ka eke ki te rima. I te tau 1999
ka eke ki te tuaono. I te tau 2002 i eke ki te mea tuawhitu ng ā tūru Māori, ngā tūru kua
whakatahangia m ō te iwi M āori, me k ī, m ō ng ā kaip ōti M āori. Ko au tētahi kua
waimaria ki te whiwhi i t ētahi tūru i raro i t ērā o ng ā korowai. Ēngari, mai i t ēnei wiki
tonu nei, i te Mane o t ēnei wiki tae r ā nō ki te 24 o H ūrae, koin ā te 4 marama kua
whakatahangia kia taea ai e Te Ao M āori te whakawhitiwhiti mai i t ētahi taha o te
taiapa, ki tētahi taha o te taiapa.
Nā, ko te mate k ē o t ēnei o ng ā kaupapa, me k ī, ko ng ā tūru M āori ka puta n ā te
tokomaha o te hunga ka r ēhita, me k ī, ki runga i te r ārangi Māori. Nō reira, i t ēnei wā
kia mōhio mai koe, e ai ki ng ā kōrero e 56 paih ēneti kei runga i te M āori roll, ka mutu,
ko te toenga kei runga i te general roll. M ā te 56 paih ēneti i runga i te M āori roll ka
whiwhi i Te Ao M āori ko ng ā tūru e whitu. N ō reira, m ēnā ka whai haere koe i t ērā
āhuatanga kia haere katoa mai Te Ao Māori ki runga i te rārangi Māori, ka 12, ka 14 pea
ngā tūru ka waihotia ake m ō Te Ao Māori. M ēnā ka eke ki t ērā kātahi ka raruraru te
taha ki te N āhinara, ka raruraru te taha ki te Reip a i te mea, ka taka mai ki runga i te
āhuatanga o te r ōpū kotahi hei tohu ko t ēhea te Kāwanatanga o te r ā. Koinei ki a au nei
te whakatinanatanga o Te Tiriti o Waitangi i te wā i whakaarohia mai ai e ngā mātua kia
pērā rawa te āhuatanga o Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
Koinei te tino kaupapa, kia whai mana te tohu o Te Ao Māori i roto i ngā nekeneke o
tēnei o ng ā Whare P āremata i runga i t ēnei o ng ā whenua. He āhua uaua te noho ā-
tokotoru ahakoa kua noho mātou a Pāti Māori nei i te taha o tētahi Kāwanatanga. I tēnei
wā ko N āhinara ēngari i t ōna mutunga mai ēhara i te mea, kai a koe te mana hei
whakakāhore rānei, hei tautoko rānei i tētahi o ngā whāinga o te Kāwanatanga. Nō reira,
ko tāku ko te k ī atu, M āori mā, tū Māori māi, hoki mai ki te r ārangi Māori kei reira te
oranga, me k ī, o ng ā tūru Māori, tuatahi, tuarua, m ēnā ka whai tonu i t ērā huarahi, ka
riro mā tētahi Pāti Māori e whakatau te Kāwanatanga ka tū mai ki konei.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: In this job for life!

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Kai te rongo ake i te Hōnore Winitana Pita e mea ana, ā,
he pai tonu tērā kia noho a Te Ururoa i roto i tōna mahi mō ake nei. Ko tāku ki a ia he rā
8990 General Debate 27 Mar 2013
tōna, koia tētahi i whaiwhai haere i ngā tūru Māori. Ko au tētahi o āna kaitautoko i te wā
i tono ia mō Te Tai Tokerau. I nāianei kua peke taiapa a te H ōnore Winitana Pita, kāore
ia i te pīrangi ki ngā tūru Māori kua waihotia ake ki te taha. Nō reira, ka hoki mai tērā ki
te ngaungau i tana nono ā te w ā. Ko t āku, ko te k ī atu e koe, e koe, kua hoki mai t ēnei
kaupapa o te t ūru Māori ki te ngau i a koe. N ō reira, ko t āku, he tautoko i t ēnei o ng ā
kaupapa. Whā marama noa iho. E te iwi Māori maranga, tū Māori mai.
[Greetings to you, Mr Speaker. Greeti ngs to us all. I will let my M āori voice settle
the dust that is flying about in this House at this point in time. Every 5 years a census is
conducted throughout the country—every 5 years. After that a M āori Option is carried
out. Why is the M āori Option being mentioned? So that M āori ones can come from the
general roll to the M āori roll or go from the M āori roll to the general roll. The real
problem with this is that the period set aside for M āori to transfer from one roll to the
other is just 4 months—only 4 months. If a M āori person does not switch over in that
period, his or her name will remain on that roll  for perhaps two elections. That is a big
issue for the ones who are Māori voters.
The Māori seats have a history, an old one. In 1967 there were four M āori seats—
four. In 1996 it reached five. In 19 99 it rose to six. In 2002 the M āori seats reached
seven. Those were the seats set aside for the M āori people, let us say, for the M āori
voters. I was one of the lucky ones to get a seat under that cloak. But from this week, the
Monday of this week until 24 July, that is the 4 months set aside so that M āoridom can
cross from one paddock to the other.
The problem with this is with the number of seats that will be  gained by the huge
number that will register, let us say, on the M āori roll. So at this moment you must
understand that according to  what has been stated, 56 percent are on the M āori roll,
with the rest being on the genera l roll. By having 56 percent on the M āori roll,
Māoridom will get seven seats. Therefore, if you follow that trend and all of M āoridom
go on to the Māori roll, 12 or 14 seats perhaps will be set aside for Māoridom. If that is
achieved, then National and Labour will be in trouble because it will come down to the
situation of one party deciding  who the Government of the day  will be. That, to me, is
the implementation of the Treaty of Waitangi  at the time when the elders considered
that it be like that.
This is the real purpose, in that M āoridom will have credibility in the mechanisms of
the Houses of Parliament, and in  this country. It is somewh at difficult as a threesome
even though we of this M āori Party are with a Government. At this point in time it is
National, but at the end of it all it is not as though y ou have the mandate to oppose or
endorse any aims of Government. Therefore, I say M āoridom, rise up, Māoridom, come
back to the M āori roll, firstly. Secondly, if we follow that to its conclusion, it will be a
Māori Party that will determine the Government.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: In this job for life!

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: I can hear the Rt Hon Winsto n Peters saying that it will
be great if Te Ururoa remains there doing his work for ever. I say to him that his day
has arrived. He was one that went after M āori seats. I was one of his supporters when
he sought the Te Tai Tokerau seat. But now  the Hon Winston Peters has jumped the
fence. He does not want any M āori seats. He has abandoned them. That will come back
to bite his buttocks in the future. I say to  him, take that, good job. This matter about
Māori seats has come back to bite you. Theref ore, I support this matter. Only 4 months.
Rise up, the Māori people, stand Māori like.]

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: What an absolutely
shocking day for the Labour Party! In the House today Labour members completely lost
it and blew it. What you saw bubbling to the surface was the manifestation of all the
frustration, all the tensions, and everything that is wrong with the Labour Party. What
27 Mar 2013 General Debate 8991
you saw was its chief whip and his buddy Tre vor Mallard trying to lure the Prime
Minister into a point of orde r contest, and they lost. They thought they had set the trap;
they blew it completely.
Trevor Mallard showed that he has not got the mental toughness for politics. Chris
Hipkins showed that he is not up to it. It was disgraceful to see the chief Labour Party
whip swearing with the most profane language at the Speaker as he left the Chamber,
and I hope that that is  going to be followed up. Meanwhil e, the lack of discipline is
showing as Labour members are tweeting abuse about the Speaker. I reckon that is a
breach of privilege. You could see how angry those members were by the way they left
the Chamber. Maryan Street completely lost  it. David Shearer wa s absolutely furious
because he has lost control of his—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We have a point of order.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I know this member is new to the House, but you cannot
refer to people leaving the Chamber and not being here. It is the oldest rule in the
book—it is the oldest in the book. You cannot do that.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: No, you know that is wrong.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: No, I know it is right.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member cannot—[ Interruption] No, I do not need any
assistance. The member cannot refer to other members who have left the Chamber. But,
equally, it is a very dangerous precedent to be bringing the Speaker into this debate.
Would the member please continue.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Well, Mr Speaker, I think the House gets the
drift: Labour has imploded. I saw Mr Shearer at 6 o’clock this morning running half-
naked in a singlet and shorts down The Terr ace. I am not sure whether he was running
from the right, the left, or the careerist left —he was running faster than the last person
who got invited up for a coffee by Mrs Ki ng’s boarder—but he looked like a man who
was frightened. I can tell you that when you are in trouble, you ge nerally go back to
your support base for succour. Well, I can tell you that the Labour Party cannot do that.
If you read The Standard you will read a post by someone called Eddie, a lady who
used to work in Michael Cullen’s office, and she clearly lays out wh at is happening in
the Labour Party at the moment . You have got the right, yo u have got the left, and you
have got the careerist left—and you have got a few who are gett ing run over in the
middle. This shows that that is the party that really does not know where it is going.
I can tell you where Labour is going. It is going nowhere, because Mr Shearer cannot
remember a thing. How are we ever going to  trust him to run the economy when he
does not even know where his own personal su rplus is? How can we trust a man whose
brain fades are so bad that he cannot reme mber that Labour campaigned in 2011 that it
was going to get rid of GST on fruit and vegeta bles? In fact, David Shearer himself said
that GST has to be repealed. Now he is saying: “Oh, I don’t actua lly know.” When you
ask him about the Mighty River Power buy-back , he cannot commit. He cannot tell you
whether they are going to buy those shares back or not—he cannot commit. When he
was asked by his union base whether he w ould support unions in the Ports of Auckland
dispute, what did he say? He said: “I’m sorry, I can’t commit.” David Shearer is Bill
Rowling for the 21st century writ large, and it is a disaster for the Labour Party. It would
be a disaster for New Zealand, and Kiwis will not put up with it.
Meanwhile, we have got John Key, a ma n with a great career background, a man
who has led us through very di fficult financial times to a point where the only country
in the OECD with higher growth is the Australians, by 0.1 percent. We had better
economic growth last year than the US, Europe, Canada, and Japan. We are on the right
track. We have got a plan. Read the Busi ness Growth Agenda. It shows where the
8992 General Debate 27 Mar 2013
country is going. It shows the 300-plus initiat ives that we put in place. Why are people
going to pick someone as shambolic as Shear er and his three factions over John Key,
who is leading a united National Party? I can tell you what. Labour members can say all
they want, but they know it is the truth. We are on the right track to lead New Zealand
into a great future.
I ask New Zealanders to look at where the country is going, look at our record over
the past 4½ years, look at how John Key has taken us through the toughest of times,
look at the path ahead, and look at the decisions we have made around education,
infrastructure, law and order, and the cour ts. The only thing that Labour members have
said that they might do is take GST off fru it and vegetables. They lost it in the House
today. It was an absolute disgrace. Frankly, it reflected very, very poorly on Parliament.
I think it shames us all as parliamentarians. I rest my case.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: When Jonathan Coleman got to his feet,
I thought he was going to get up and apologi se for the appalling failures in the two
portfolios that he is responsible for in this House. [ Interruption] The first portfolio, Mr
Coleman, is defence. You know, in 12 short months, you have achieved the lowest
morale ever in the New Zealand Defence Force on record in its own surveys, and the
loss of 1,000 skilled, experienced, and qua lified service personnel from the armed
forces to the extent that we have got to get Aussie sailors to put our new ships to sea out
from Devonport, in his electorate. He woul d know that—he would know that. And we
have seen the worst ever attrition rate in the Defence Force, at over 21 percent.
But I want to talk about his other failure s—his failures in the area of being State
services Minister. Last Friday we saw th e biggest ever release of confidential
information—the biggest ever breach of priv acy in the history of this country. Ninety-
eight thousand people in Christ church had confidential information about their property
and repairs released by the Earthquake  Commission—98,000 people who would dearly
love, each of them, to have the informa tion about their own property, because the
Earthquake Commission will not give them in formation about their own property. This
was a massive breach of confidentiality.
And it was not the first; in fact, it was the seventh such breach in the last year. Let us
look at the track record: at  the Accident Compensation Corporation, 6,700 files were
released to Bronwyn Pullar; at the Inland Revenue Department, 6,300 pieces of personal
information about tax records were released; and at Work and Income, 7,000 documents
were released, including documents, highl y confidential and hi ghly personal, about
children in care. Then there is Novopay. To add insult to injury, not only is it not paying
people but also it is releas ing information about their pa y to people who should not get
it.
John Key stood up in this House yesterday and said there is no systemic problem.
You know, “Planet Key” is an odd place, where you can get a comment like that—
seven major breaches, literally tens of t housands of people having their confidential
information released, and John Key says “no sy stemic problem”. Well, that is not what
the Privacy Commissioner is saying. She de scribed last year—this is in a press
statement—as the year of the data breach. Th at is what the Privacy Commissioner said.
This year already there have been 10 times  as many releases of confidential documents
as there were in the whole of  last year. I want to know wh at this Government is doing
about it. Why is no action being taken to protect private information about individuals?
Colmar Brunton did a poll, and it found that  two-thirds of New Zealanders did not
trust their information to be kept c onfidential by Government agencies. This
Government is responsible for that, but th is Government is pretending not to be
accountable, and is not accountable. Why is th at? It is because Ministers themselves
have been complicit with the release of personal information. Paula Bennett misused her
27 Mar 2013 General Debate 8993
ministerial powers to release information taken from the personal files of two
beneficiaries who had had the temerity to criticise her policies. Beware, New
Zealanders, this is a Governme nt with Ministers who will delve into personal files and
release them publicly. And when she was censured by the Human Rights Commission
about that, she said she disa greed with its view and she would not rule out doing it
again.
Then we have got Judith Collins. ACC released, wrongly, 6,700 files, and then Judith
Collins’ office released the name—not released  but leaked the name—of the person it
had sent them to wrongly, Bronwyn Pullar. When Bronwyn Pullar got in an advocate by
the name of Michelle Boag, president of the Labour Party, to speak on her behalf, the
emails that Michelle Boag sent to the Minister were also leaked. Do you know what she
said—and I shall finish with this—

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speake r. I do not believe that Michelle
Boag is the leader of the Labour Party. The National Party—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And I am sure it was a slip of the tongue. But it is debatable; it is
not a valid point of order.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: I shall finish my last sentence. This is what Michelle Boag, the
former president of the National Party, sa id: “When you can’t send  a communication to
a Government minister without fearing that the privacy of that co mmunication is going
to be breached, that’s very, ve ry dangerous.” That is the qu ote. That is what she said
about her own party.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: We live in a very complex
and fast-paced world. We juggle technologies , new ideas, and different philosophies.
That is the noisy buzz and detail of our da ily lives, and, actually, much of what we
debate in Parliament—and certainly questi on time today was a good example of the
irrelevancies from the Opposition. In reality, only a few things really matter. Only a few
things really change our lives, and if we can  get them right, all th e rest is flotsam and
jetsam. What we want is healthy families,  we want educated young people, we want
safe communities, and we want jobs. To make all these things happen, we need a secure
economic future. In New Zealand under this  John Key - led National Government we
can tick all those boxes. We are focused on th e things that absolutely matter to all New
Zealanders.
In an unstable and insecure world—and we watch on the television and see the
financial ructions right across the world—t his Government is managing our finances
amazingly well, and our economy is growing. Our health system is remarkably
effective, our crime rate is down, and the quality of our education right across the
country is improving.
Of course, just like everybody else around the world, we have had to tighten our
belts. This Government made a deliberate de cision to protect the most vulnerable
families. We have kept all the establishe d entitlements, including things like Working
for Families, and increased superannuation payments as we work towards getting into
surplus from 2014 or 2015. We are one of the ve ry few developed countries that has not
increased public debt, and that puts us in a very strong economic position.
Our prudent economic management has made  things easier for all New Zealanders,
because despite the global financial crisis and the high dollar, our economy has grown
in nine out of the last 10 quarters, which is an almost unheard-of achievement in the
developed world right now. The latest figures show that we  are growing at 3 percent,
and in my home town of Christchurch we ar e growing at 7.5 percent. We have never
seen that sort of growth anywhere in New Zealand ev er before. The New Zealand
economy is growing faster than Canada’s economy, faster than the US economy, much
faster than Japan’s economy, and much fast er than the UK’s econom y, and it is even
8994 General Debate 27 Mar 2013
trumping the EU, whose economy is actually  shrinking. Our growth forecasts are
steady, and they are continuing to be better than most countries going forward.
New Zealanders are doing OK because we are managing to keep mortgage rates
low—the lowest for 45 years. Some of us remember buying our first homes when our
mortgage rates were in the 20 percent range. Keeping interest rates low for homeowners
and landlords helps everyone keep their household budgets down. Th e tax cuts across
the board mean that most people have grea ter take-home pay and those who are getting
superannuation are also getting the benefits of that take-home pay.
But, more important, this Government has a relentless focus on work. We understand
how important it is to help people get into work. We know that in the normal course of
events jobs come and go, but good jobs unde rpin the health and the wealth of our
nation, and we are working really hard to  make our economy more competitive and
more productive so that businesses can add to the 60,000 jobs created in the last 2 years.
So, as we focus on the detail of our business in  debates, let us make sure we continue to
do the really important stuff well, because  keeping families healthy, educating our
children, keeping our communities safe, and ensuring ongoing economic security is
actually what it is all about.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: The previous speaker, Nicky Wagner, talked about a
secure economic future, but she missed a major thing out, and that is because this
Government does not understand that a secure economic future depends on a well-
managed environment. That is the basis for economic prosperity and our well-being.
Instead, we have a Government that is hitting on the environm ent over and over and
over again. It is dismantling our envi ronmental legislation, stripping out the
environmental principles from the Res ource Management Act, making it easier for
people to mine on conservation land, and maki ng it harder for people to have a say in
protecting their neighbourhoods and the pl aces they love from inappropriate
development. It is a Government that know s the price of everything and the value of
nothing.
We have seen that in the loss of 140 jobs—another 140 jobs—from the Department
of Conservation this week, because of funding cuts and continuing fiscal pressure on the
department. There is a huge lo ss of professional expertise in biodiversity, in recreation
management, in historic heritage manageme nt, and in practical skills like predator
control in these job losses. Bu t there is something even more troubling in the staff cuts
and the new structure that the Department of  Conservation is rolling out. It is because
there is a major change in the department’s  strategic direction. It is changing from
allowing commercial activity on conservatio n land, such as tourism, when it is
compatible with conservation values, to enab ling it. That is confirmed in the briefing
papers to the incoming, recycled Minister of Conservation, where we see a comment
that the department has been charged, along with the Ministry of Business, Innovation
and Employment, with identifying options for realising greater value from international
visitors’ use of public cons ervation lands. Is that what we are going to see on
conservation lands in the future? Is that a way of realising gr eater value—having
McDonald’s outlets at the start of the Route burn Track? That is what the department is
potentially about with the new structure.
The “Minister of Everything”, Steven J oyce, has directed, along with the Prime
Minister and Nick Smith, th at the Ministry of Busine ss, Innovation and Employment
and the Department of Conservation work  on enabling more commercial development
of conservation land. What does that mean ? It means more mines, more habitat
destruction, more inappropriate developm ent, like McDonald’s outlets, potentially
happening on conservation land. That is beca use this Government does not recognise
the need to invest in nature and environm ental protection if we want a strong economy
27 Mar 2013 General Debate 8995
and long-term prosperity for New Zealand. Th at is because this Government does not
realise that overseas, people are questioni ng whether the “100% Pure New Zealand”
brand is real. We need to make it real and give it more integrity.
This Government has a frontier attitude towa rds the environment. It sees nature as
something to exploit. Its vision for Aotearoa  New Zealand is to open up our oceans to
deep-sea drilling. Its vision is to sell off our  energy companies and use the revenue that
that generates to put $400 million into subsidising agribusiness through big, new
irrigation schemes. That is $400 million into promoting irrigation, when it will not put
more than $150 million into the protection of  natural heritage through the Department
of Conservation.
This is a Government that is in its fifth year in power and we have not seen a single
new national park, despite National saying that  it would establish Kauri National Park
in Northland, despite it saying it would investig ate a national park in the Waitakeres. It
has been slow on protecting M āui’s dolphins, and that specie s is potentially on a slow
slide to extinction. We have got a Minister  of Conservation who turns down a tiny
marine reserve in Akaroa Harbour, less than 12 percent of the har bour, despite the fact
that there is only one postage stamp - sized reserve on the whole east coast of the South
Island. It is a Government that is toxic to the environment in its changes to legislation,
changes to the Resource Management Act, and changes to the Crown Minerals Act, and
in its starving the Department  of Conservation of funds and in the major change in the
department’s strategic direction.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I think it is quite clear that New Zealanders
have totally and utterly woken up to what is  coming out of the Labour benches and, of
course, from our friends across there in th e watermelon patch. They have totally woken
up to the sort of double-headed approach that is akin to throwing enough mud and
hoping a little bit of it sticks, and, also, scaring everyone into thinking there is some sort
of a crisis out there. It seems to me that th at approach is very much about saying: “If we
can, scare people into thinking we are a viable alternative—so let’s manufacture up a
crisis.” It seems they have  gone a little bit quiet on the idea of a manufacturing crisis,
but it does not stop them trying to manufacture their own crisis.
Well, there is something very scary all right. There is something very scary about
parties on the other side of th e House, and that is the prospect to New Zealanders of a
Labour-led, Labour-Green Government with  one Russel Norman with his finger on
Treasury’s xerox. That is what  we call “A for Armageddon”, a nd that is pretty scary to
New Zealanders.
What is just as scary, I think, is the brai n fade of the Leader of the Opposition, one
David Shearer. This is the same person who has $50,000-plus—we are not sure how
much it is; he does not seem too keen to tell us, but it is at least $50,000—in a foreign
bank account, and it seems that he cannot reme mber to put it on hi s pecuniary interests
return. I think that we can forgive people for making an honest mistake. But then we ask
ourselves: did he do this in 2009? Yes. Did he  do this in 2010? Yes. Did he do this in
2011? Yes. Did he do this in 2012? Yes. Did he pay his tax every year on that money?
Yes. So one could ask themselves whether this is an honest mistake—I do not know.
But this is the man who would be Prime Mini ster; this is the ma n who wants his hands
on Treasury’s money. I say to you that he seems to have a problem when other members
in this House have issues around memory a nd money, but it seems that it is sweet as a
nut when it involves him. Well, that does not  sit too well with Kiwis, and they have
worked that out.
Some other inconsistencies that we might  want to consider when throwing stones
around a glass house is that La bour is quite happy to promote one Hon Shane Jones—a
good bloke, but the Auditor-General did not ha ve too much good to say in her report.
8996 General Debate 27 Mar 2013
But suddenly, of course, the Labour Party want s to take the Government down when in
the Auditor-General’s report into the Skyc ity Casino there was some discussion about
how the process could have been better. When  one looks at those two reports, I think it
is quite evident to see where the weight of evidence lies there, but it seems what is good
for the goose is not necessarily good for the gander.
We can also look back to the 2011 elec tion campaign. I was watching with great
interest as the Hon Phil Goff, doing his very best to keep th at sinking ship afloat, talked
about the fact that the 2011 campaign wa s a referendum on asset sales—it was a
referendum on asset sales. I think we will all remember that, and I am certainly sure that
Labour Party members would remember it.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: And most people backed a party that opposed asset sales—right or
wrong?

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: It just so happens, Mr Clark, that  when Labour lost the election, all
of a sudden the faith it had in New Zeal anders and what was the referendum means
nothing, because all of a sudden it wants anot her one. It gets its friends over in the
Greens to pay a few people to scratch up a few signatures, and away it goes.
It seems to me that when we are throwing mud, one must be very careful that one is
not throwing it at a fan, because it does tend to blow back in one’s face. That is what we
are seeing time and time again here from a La bour Party and from a leadership that is
scrambling to find its feet. If we look at the Labour Party, I think we can be quite
confident that the Labour caucus has suppor t for its leader—absol utely confident in
that—just the same as we can see that the Labor Party caucus in Australia has great faith
in its leader, Julia Gillard. There is a good reason for that, and the reason is that they
stand only themselves as a candidate. There is no one else running against them. It is
hard to lose an election in that circumstan ce. I bet you that Mr Shearer hopes that that
would happen in a general election, but I cannot see that happening any time soon.
I submit that there is a stark difference between the National-led Government and the
Labour and Green benches. Th is is a disciplined Nationa l-led Government that is
focused on what matters to Kiwis: th e economy, and managing the Government’s
finance. The two-headed monster that we se e on the other side of the House has a plan,
and it is so cunning that you could pin a tail on it and call it a Cunliffe.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: It is a basic, f undamental principle
of our democracy, of our country, that data  and information about any individual that
are collected by a Government, whether it is a department, a ministry, or an agency,
should be kept confidential, and that the Government agency can be trusted—can be
trusted—to treat your information within a se t of guidelines, that your personal details
will not be accidentally emailed to a complete stranger, as we have seen with the latest
breach, at the Earthquake Commi ssion, and that your sensitive information will not be
shared inappropriately or ha nded to the media to make a political point. How can the
public of New Zealand trust a Government that allows systemic breaches across
multiple departments and agencies to occur, and when they occur the Prime Minister
behaves as if it is all not a problem and he is indifferent and dismissive, as we have seen
this week?
This is an extremely serious matter, and it is a matter of public trust. It requires a
serious response and an acknowledgment that th ese issues need to be addressed not just
on a department by department or a case by case basis but right across the Government.
It requires a systemic response, and it will require the Prime Minister of this country
and all of the Ministers on that  side of the House to take off their blinke rs, get out of
their horses and carts, stop their jokes, and get into the 21 st century. The Prime Minister
really had better smarten up, because his pathetic responses are being met with
27 Mar 2013 General Debate 8997
derision—derision and disbelief—from an information and communications technology
community that is aghast at the ignorance and indifference that he is showing.
This is not just about an i ndividual’s human e rror; this is 2013 and it should not be
happening. There should be systems in place  to prevent these things happening, to
prevent human error. In the last year, as  Phil Goff pointed out, more than 120,000 New
Zealanders have had their privacy breached by this Government’s incompetence, its
head in the sand attitude, or its blatant disr egard for individuals’ privacy. Phil Goff read
them out—seven different ministries and agencies. Hekia Parata and Paula Bennett were
two Ministers caught out releasing private correspondence and private information.
The private sector has warned repeatedly that New Zealand has a major problem with
information security, and a strategy released  late last year by a group of IT security
professionals said that “While technologica l innovation is high within the New Zealand
market, the national spend on educating, tr aining and developing skilled technical
personnel is surprisingly low, creating an im balance and directly contributing to the
fragility and vulnerability of  our nations IT systems.” If  that is not a significant
warning, I do not know what is. Yesterday the chief executive officer of the Institute of
IT Professionals, Paul Matthews, said that the Earthquake Commission had failed
Security 101 and that it was mickey mouse st uff that such sensitive information could
be sent so easily to an out side person. It is not rocket science. SEEMail, which David
Shearer referenced yesterday in the House, is just one secure electronic system. Why
has it not been mandated across all Gove rnment agencies and ministries? As I
understand it, it is not mandatory; it is an opt-out system. The point is that what we need
to know is that there is a basic system acr oss all agencies, and if there is sensitive
material to be handled, then it is critical . There are plenty of options out there. The
private sector has plenty of options, if the Government wa s willing to ask it. Simple
checks—you send the email with  an attachment and it bounc es back, checking that you
really want to send it.
Last year two-thirds of New Zealanders said that they did not trust Government
departments to protect their information. I wonder what they would be saying now. We
have to treat this seriously. I have got a member’s bill that will come before this House
in the next few months. It is called the Elec tronic Data Safety Bill. It sets up a special
commission of inquiry across Government agen cies. It is a very serious matter. In the
absence of a joined-up strategy for our data security, I urge everyone to support it.

items.speaker: AARON GILMORE
items.text: The irony. We heard the last speaker, Clare
Curran, talk about data protection and secur ity. That member is the same one who goes
on to her own party’s forum and censures he r own members about what they can and
cannot say. It is hypocrisy for th e Labour Party to be talking about the ability to protect
data when the information of its own party members and donors could not be kept secret
from the public and was released.
There is a comment that that member did make that is an extremely serious matter
and one of public interest, and that is the matter of the Leader of the Opposition and his
ability to talk of public trust and welfare and worrying about where his own money is or
is not. I want to walk through a few things. Mr Shearer returned to New Zealand some
time in 2008 to run for public office and be th e MP for Mt Albert. What I understand is
that at that time Mr Shearer may have appl ied for an exemption that exists for overseas
returnees and migrants coming back to New Zealand, which grants an exemption of up
to 4 years for income tax, including inte rest income. In 2006 the Inland Revenue
Department put those rules in place. Mr Shea rer is completely entitled to do that. In
2009 he ran for public office, and we are now told in 2013 that while Mr Shearer was
filling in his tax returns for the 2012-13 ye ar he understands that due to some
8998 General Debate 27 Mar 2013
information he discovered he needs to have filled in the pecuniary interests register,
which actually has the information about interest income.
I want to talk through an interesting thing. You are requ ired to disclose interest
income to the Inland Revenue Department in  New Zealand only if you have more than
$200 in net after-tax income. Mr  Shearer has publicly stated  that the deposit he has is
contained at the Chase Bank in Manhattan. He is on record as saying that. He is on
record as saying that it is more than  $50,000. If you go to the Chase Bank and you ask
them what the deposit rates are for vari ous items, you have to have over $400,000 in
that bank account to have an amount that should be disclosed under Inland Revenue
Department rules in New Zealand—over $400,000. The interest rate at the Chase Bank
is 0.05 percent per annum—0.05 percent per annum. The deposit is not $50,000; it is
probably likely to be $400,000. This information is publicly available.  If I can go and
find it, why can Mr Shearer not front up to the people of New Zealand, be honest with
them, and disclose the information we are talking about? I do not have any problems
with Mr Shearer being a multimillionaire, bu t he should be open with the members of
the Labour Party and the people of New Zeal and about how much he has hidden away.
Mr Shearer needs to come clean.
When you look at the information on the other si de of the fence, we have a leader in
John Key. We have heard many of the Oppos ition spokespeople moaning and groaning
about the differences between Mr Key and Mr Shearer. Well, I say that we have a Prime
Minister in Mr Key who is committed to rebuilding Christchurch. On the record today, I
want to talk in my last littl e bit about what is actually ha ppening in Christchurch in the
rebuild there. [ Interruption] I am sure that the lady over there, Ms Dalziel, may touch
on this in a very short period of time.
What I want to talk about is the commi tment to rebuilding Burwood Hospital, and
over $200 million and over 500 jobs moving into my community in north-east
Christchurch. I want to talk about the building of new subdivisions and hundreds of new
jobs in and around the Prestons subdivision. I want to talk about the potential building
of a water park that 20,000 people signe d a petition supporting. The Labour Party
patently said it was not for it  until public record and the mayor were. I want to talk here
about a retirement village that is committed to building hundreds of units and investing
hundreds of millions of dollars.
That is the difference between Labour a nd National. We are for jobs, building our
community, and being open and honest with our mistakes. The O pposition, led by Mr
Shearer, is being deliberately evasive by not coming out and telling us the information
about whether Mr Shearer took advantage of the 4-year tax exemption he was offered
and had the ability to use unde r Inland Revenue Department rules, and, if so, whether it
is only this year that he is required to declare his income, as required by Inland Revenue
Department rules, and whether it is actually $400,000, as I believe it is. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: We should have had a
snap debate yesterday as a result of the privacy breach by the Earthquake Commission.
It met every test. However, what was re lied on was the Privacy Commissioner noting
that the Earthquake Commission had taken an honest and open approach to the breach. I
agree with that. If that was all that had happened—what happened on Friday—I would
not have called for a snap debate. Then it was also said that the commissioner would be
following up to make sure that similar breaches cannot occur in the future. I want to tell
the House what else the Pr ivacy Commissioner said in her release: “The Privacy
Commissioner Marie Shroff said today”—and this was on Friday—“that public sector
agencies needed to have stronger controls  in place when hand ling spread sheets of
personal information. ‘The EQC breach is ye t another incident involving inadvertent
disclosure of large amounts of personal in formation on a spread sheet. We hope that
27 Mar 2013 General Debate 8999
agencies are starting to realise that they should have stronger controls in place to help to
prevent these types of mistakes. But they cl early have a way to go yet. I think it has
reached the stage where the public need some  further reassurance,’ Marie Shroff said.
‘So I am considering writing to the State Se rvices Commissioner and all public sector
chief executives, asking them to tell me what precautions they have put or are putting in
place to help prevent inadvertent emailing of client information on spread sheets.’”
Then she said the bit that was relied on yesterday, and then she said this: “There are
real people behind the information that govern ment holds, and we al l have the right to
expect that our information will be stro ngly protected.” That is the issue. The
Government can take the Crosby/Textor clas sic approach of atta cking the messenger to
divert attention from the real problem, but  this will not go away. The role of the
parliamentary Opposition is to hold the Government to account, but when we are denied
access to the tools our Standing Orders pr ovide for that purpose, for unknown reasons,
the Government is let off the hook, unreasona bly so. The Prime Minister should have
been standing in the House yesterday admitti ng that the Government had failed to give
the people of New Zealand confidence that it  can be entrusted with people’s personal
information, and that is what this is all about.
Yes, there is a Christchurch issue,  and now we know that the Earthquake
Commission could easily give people a quick sn apshot of where they are up to in the
system, whether there are any hold-ups with th eir claim, what they are, and what time
frame is anticipated for their resoluti on. Not one aspect of the confidential,
commercially sensitive information needs to be released, but, of course, that is the
one—the Crosby/Textor approach—that th e Minister for Cant erbury Earthquake
Recovery focuses on, to avoid fronting the real question, which is why people do not
know what is holding them up, and why the Earthquake Commission will not give them
that information. We now know that it has precisely that information.
But the bigger-picture issue is that this Government is not meeting its obligations to
provide data protection, even though it is legally and mora lly obliged to do so. Under
John Key’s watch, there have been serious  breaches of New Zealanders’ private
information at the Ministry of Social  Development, ACC, the Inland Revenue
Department, Work and Income, Novopay, the Department of Corrections, and now the
Earthquake Commission. This is not just a simp le case of human error. Of course there
was human error, but it is not good enough to say that we have all sent an email or a text
message by mistake at some point. We are not all responsible for massive amounts of
personal data. It is not good enough to say that  it was one file sent to one person. It
contained over 80,000 separate entries c overing 98,000 claims. It is not good enough to
say that this is like putting the wrong address on an envelope. It is not. The Government
is responsible for receiving and handli ng massive amounts of personal information,
which can be transmitted in a nanosecond. That  is why we have data-protection laws.
You could not stuff 80,000 pieces of informati on into an envelope to wrongly address.
That is the point of data protection.
The latest breach shows that there is cl ear evidence of a serious and widespread
problem with the security of our Governme nt information systems. That is why the
Prime Minister of New Zealand must take responsibility.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: It was interesting to hear this week that Labour is
considering going back on one of its major el ection platforms of last election: GST off
fresh fruit and vegetables. “If we can’t afford policies”—we heard Mr Shearer say—
“then they will have to go.” Now, apparentl y, “GST off fresh fruit and [vegetables] is
one of the things we’re looking at.” Is it not amazing?
As I recall, that was one of the major election promises of 2011, pushed by Phil Goff.
He stood there, he roared, and he bellowed: “Labour’s plan is a bol d one. It’s a game-
9000 General Debate 27 Mar 2013
changer. It’s about fairness,”. He gnashed  his teeth, he thundered, and he went puce
with rage. We had Mr Cunliffe standing on t op of a bus with a l oud hailer roaring that
this was going to bring social  justice to New Zealand. We had Mr Parker, and I am not
quite sure—I do not think he was convinced  about it. He did not say too much. Mr
Parker I am not too sure about, but Mr Sh earer certainly said that if the goods and
services tax did not apply to  fresh fruit and vegetables, then they would be much
cheaper for ordinary New Zealanders.
Now we hear that maybe that is not going to work after all. It was going to cost about
$317 million—that was the guess—and Mr Shearer says: “Well, can we do it all? I
doubt whether we can. We are going to have to reprioritise.” So he  is prevaricating,
massaging the media, and warming us up for a climb-down on one of Labour’s key
platforms. What has happened to the Labour  Party? What has happened? This party
used to be one of conviction and principles . When Roger Douglas led the party it was
firm and it was brave, but now it seems to have a leader with a spine like a jellyfish, and
it is going back on all sorts of things. He is refusing to say what is going to happen.
I note that there are one or two coalition pr oblems ahead. It was interesting to read
the response of Labour’s poten tial coalition ally, the Mana party. One fellow, the
economic justice spokesperson—I cannot remember his name—said: “It is hard to think
of a more week-kneed, pathetic announcement.” So that is not so good for relationships
between Mana and Labour. I am not sure wh ere the Greens are on this, but I am quite
confident—and I call upon them. I call upon the Greens there to make clear their views
on what they think about GST on fresh vegetables.
Labour abandoned it because it was a crazy id ea. I mean, if it is supposed to bring
about social justice, then why would you ta ke the GST off imported pawpaws sold at
my local fruit and vegetable shop, Jack Lu m’s in Remuera? How is that going to
advance social justice in this  country? If fruit and vegeta bles, why not water? But not
bottled water—normal water. If you are goi ng to have GST off potatoes, why do you
not have it off staples like pasta? But not fancy pasta. Or  bread—plain stuff, but not
Vogel’s. Or we could have clothing—why should we not have the GST off clothing?
But not fancy clothing—school uniforms, perh aps, but not private-school uniforms. We
should take the GST off books because e ducation and moral improvement of the
country is very important—but non-fic tion books, not trashy novels; maybe New
Zealand novels—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: What about biographies?

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: —and biographies, possibly. But we would be in a terrible
tangle, and we would be undermining one of the great strengths of the GST and the tax
system in this country, complicating a beautifully simple solution.

Before I finish I did want to draw a contrast, if I could indulge the time of the House,
between Labour’s tax policy and the tax policy of this Government, which is focused

and competitive economy through welfare reform and the Business Growth Agenda. All

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: I move, That the Habeas Corpus Amendment
Bill be now read a third time . This bill promotes a fair, efficient, and modern justice
system and I am grateful for the support it has received from this House and during the
select committee process. The Justice and Electoral Committee has made minor
technical changes from the original bill as  it was introduced, but it has fundamentally
retained the status quo and its changes still protect current rights of appeal, ensuring that
this bill retains and will ach ieve its purpose: the protectio n of the “great writ”. The
“great writ” will be protected from improper use and this ensures that we have an
effective justice system. Habeas corpus is an ancient writ, requiring a person in State
detention to be brought before a judge or c ourt to determine whether their detention is
lawful. Its importance throughout history is almost unparallele d, with its first recorded
use occurring in the 14th century. It is for exactly this reason that the improper use of the
writ must be not be allowed to continue.
In 1997 the Law Commission made recommenda tions to simplify the procedure for
dealing with habeas corpus applications. The Habeas Corpus Act in 2001 implemented
the changes recommended in this report and fo r the first time formalised habeas corpus
in legislation. However, since then practical experience has revealed several anomalies
in the application of the le gislation. For example, the 2001 Act required habeas corpus
applications to be given precedence over all other court business. This left it open to
misuse in some cases. In 2007, following co nsultation with the judiciary and the
Government agencies, the Law Commission i ssued a report addressing these concerns.
The bill incorporates the changes recommended in that report.
This bill will allow the High Court or a judge of the High Cour t to be able to
dispense with the rule that habeas corpus  applications take precedence over all other
business. It will ensure the easier transfer of applications to the Family Court where
9002 Habeas Corpus Amendment Bill 27 Mar 2013
appropriate. It will provide for a judge to be able to dismiss applications that are statute
barred or use incorrect procedure, and will allow procedural improvements such as
holding pre-hearing conferences and hearings by technology au thorised by rules of the
court. These changes address issues that ha ve clogged courts, fail ed to evolve with
technological improvements, and dragged dow n the position of the “great writ”. This
bill will address these issues. I am proud that this bill fits within this Government’s
programmes to streamline our courts and ensu re they are used for their proper purpose,
and I would like to congratulate the Hon Chester Borrows on the work he has done in
our court system. It has been exemplary, and it was a great privilege to be with him
down in Westland at Whataroa courthouse.
I would like to close with this statement. Freedom from arbitrary arrest is a
fundamental right. It is vital to our health as a nation that this is protected. This bill does
not do anything to diminish the substance of this right. What it does  do is ensure that
this right is not conflated into a “get out of jail free” card for any situation. It is not. I
thank the House for its time and call on all me mbers to support this bill and to support a
fair, efficient, and modern justice system. Thank you.

items.text: Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I thought that in a moment of injustice I was going
to be deprived of an opportunity to speak in the great House on the “great writ”! So I
am very pleased to take this call on this very important piece of legislation, the Habeas
Corpus Amendment Bill. As Mr Auchinvole has rightly said, habeas corpus goes to the
heart of democracy and the sort of justice sy stem that we celebrate and enjoy in this
country. It has its origins as far back as  1215 in the Magna Carta, and the injunction
there to prevent the arbitrary arrest and dete ntion of peasants and the other citizenry by
the monarch and the feudal lords. Of course, that is as much a risk today in some
quarters as it was then, some might suspect.
It is so important to our system of justice—and I do not wish to be dramatic in saying
this—which, frankly, is under threat today. It  is not because of that member, nor, I
might add, because of the Hon Chester Borro ws, although I have some criticisms of his
performance, but because we have in New Z ealand today the worst Minister of Justice
we have had in more than a generation—a Mi nister of Justice w ho is presiding over
cuts, cutbacks, and deprivation of access to justice in a way that we have not seen in the
history of this great country. We are seeing it not just in the Family Court and we are
seeing it not just in the District Courts—and this is where Chester Borrows does know a
thing or two, because he is busily closing th em down, and he has only this week closed
down the Upper Hutt District Court, and, of  course, courts in his own region—but we
are seeing it in cuts to the budget for the Crown Law Office and the Public Defenders
Office and in a whole host of areas in legal aid. This is all adding up to a very serious
erosion of principles of justice and, most important, access to justice.
Habeas corpus has at its heart the right of citizens not only to be deprived of arbitrary
arrest and detention, but, if th at happens or is alleged to have happened, to be brought
before a court to have it tested, and this House should never lightly  interfere with the
High Court’s jurisdiction in this area. This bill creates some sensible reforms and some
expeditious measures about habeas corpus, but  let us not understate the value of it, and
let us not forget that we ha ve a justice system that, fr ankly, is under threat at the
moment and upon which more work will be required. But we will support this bill.
27 Mar 2013 Habeas Corpus Amendment Bill 9003

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: I am enjoying the passage of this
Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi Da y and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill. I
want to place on record from the outset my thanks to all of those parties in Parliament
that are supporting this bill: to my Labour colleagues, the Green Party, New Zealand
First, the Māori Party, United Future, Mana, and Brendan Horan. They have all pledged
their support for this bill, an d without it this bill would not pass through the House. It
indicates several things: the popula rity of this bill, the fact that it is common sense, and
that it restores to ordinary Kiwis the 11 pub lic holidays they expect to receive every
year.
The bill has been universally popular sin ce it was made clear that commemorations
will still occur on the same days that they always have—that is, 6 February for Waitangi
9004 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 27 Mar 2013
Day and 25 April for Anzac Day. The fact that a holiday follows on the Monday that
follows a weekend occurrence of those days is what changes. We have a bill that makes
sure that we have those 11 holidays every year. That gives those holidays the full
recognition that other holidays have.
I would like the National Party to consider its support for this bill also. In some polls
more than 80 percent of New Zealanders su pport this bill. In th e only quantitative
survey that has been done 87 percent of small and medium sized business owners are
either in support of or neutra l toward this bill. New Zealan d knows that this is a fair
idea. It makes sure that ordinary hard-w orking Kiwis get the holidays they deserve
every year. So I want the National Party to get in behind this bill.
I want John Key to get in behind this bill. His suggesti on today in Parliament that
ordinary Kiwis could not be trusted to front on Anzac Day is a disgrace. It is an outrage.
Millions of ordinary Australians turn out on Anzac Day year after year after year. Their
turnout is increasing. Mondayising has worked in Australia; it should work here too. If
ordinary Australians can turn out for commem orations, I want to think that ordinary
New Zealanders can too. For the Prime Mi nister to suggest otherwise is an
embarrassment. So just to be clear on that , for John Key’s point to hold he would have
to think that Christmas and New Year would not be held in such high regard if they fell
on a weekend. Does he not remember 2010? Did Kiwis decide on Christmas morning
that they would not get up and open their presents? Or Christians that they would not go
off to their church services, because there was a holiday 2 days later? I do not think so. I
think that is a nonsense position to take.
Ordinary Kiwis will honour these days and commemorate these days because they
are of growing importance to New Zealanders. They are about our pride and our identity
as New Zealanders, they are of growing impor tance to all of us, and they should have
the full recognition that other holidays have. As Marcus Lush said on the radio, you
would have to be the Grinch to oppose Mondayisation.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I find it a little ironic that the member

continue until morale improves” approach to garnering support.
I think it is actually a very, very fine ba lance that is looking to be achieved. I
certainly do respect the views of parties that are supporting this Holidays (Full
Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Da y) Amendment Bill, and I can actually
see why. I do not think we would have to go too far to find out why the honest Joe on
the street is going to think that having a nother long weekend is not a bad idea. But I
think for me where this discussion lands is really the significan ce and importance of
those 2 days. Waitangi Day, the founding day of the New Zealand that we know, and
Anzac Day, which has come to be a time of some sombre reflection and
commemoration for those who have lost their lives in the service of the freedom that we
all enjoy today, are things that  as an ex-serviceman I feel very, very strongly about. I
know that that is a view shared by ma ny across the RSAs, many of those returned
servicemen, but also their fa milies and their loved ones around them, and that to me is
where the balance needs to rest.
An argument has been raised around the fact  that if Anzac Day, for example, fell on
a Saturday, that would in no way be devalu ed by the fact that the following Monday
would become a holiday. Well, I think the la w of the jungle would suggest otherwise,
and people would see the opportunity to lash th e kayak to the roof rack, put the trailer
on, and head for the beach and so on and so forth.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is that what you’d do?
27 Mar 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9005

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I do not have to, Ms King; I live at the beach, so feel free to come
and visit at some stage. I believe that that member’s caucus sometimes comes up to see

a few photos, and leaving again, so feel free to call in to my house just down the road
when you do. You will notice that I do not need  to lash the kayak on the roof rack,

But coming back to the bill—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: But why are other New Zealande rs so dumb if that’s what

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: It is not a question of New Zealanders being dumb. I think that the
argument being run by the Opposition is a futile one. I think that the bill actually
deserves a better discussion. When I think about the importance of those days, Anzac
Day and Waitangi Day, and the significance of those days, as a member of Parliament
for Northland, I can vouch for the importance of Waitangi Day, certainly to locals but, I
believe, also to all New Zeala nders. It is a day of signifi cance. So the balance becomes
whether this devalues those days. My belief  is, when talking to servicemen, the people
who fought for the country, that that is how they  see it. If it is just simply because hard-
working Kiwis deserve another day off, then I think that balance tips too far. No one
wants to deny Kiwis the opportunity of a day off—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: You do.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: No, that is not the ca se. But it is around the c ontext in which we are
doing it and using these 2 most significant da ys for New Zealand as the meat in the
sandwich to achieve that purpose. I do not believe that that balance has been met.
It was absolutely pointed to by the leader of that memb er’s party this afternoon at
question time, when he questioned the Prime Minister as to why the tourism industry
was so supportive of this bill. Why would tourism be so interested in supporting the
bill? Because tourism is about holidays. Tourism is about relaxing, going away, and

believe we are advancing, that th ere is a very real risk that  in Mondayising, we lose the
value and the significance of the commemora tion of those days. Are people seriously
going to celebrate Anzac Day on a Saturday  and then somehow—I do not know. What
happens to the Monday? I do not think so. As I said, the balance becomes those who
fought for the freedoms that this country enjoys and the founding of this nation. We
should not devalue those days.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: I will take a short call on the Holidays (Full

items.text: Order! Sorry to the member. I am trying to

items.text: Thank you. As I was saying, I would like to address the
proposed commencement date in clause 2. The bill as introduced would have come into
force the day after the Royal assent was given,  and that is good. It is axiomatic that if
Parliament enacts legislation, then it shou ld be implemented. But although that is
obvious, it does not always happen. The bill as reported back would come into force on
1 January 2014—9 months from now. On the f ace of it, that may not seem to be a
problem, as the first occasion on which the la w would have practicable effect would be
on Anzac Day in 2015, but long commencement dates can have unintended
consequences.
9006 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 27 Mar 2013
It has been the habit of previous Parliaments to write Governments of the day a blank
cheque, but at least this bill is not open-ended. We have allowed Acts to be brought into
force by Order in Council and ye t not specified any default da te. For example, part of
the Summary Proceedings Amendment Act 1976 is still not in force, 37 years after
Parliament passed the law. There are over 30 such Acts on the books, not in force and
with an open-ended, indefinite commencement date. Things can go wrong with definite
but long commencement dates. For example, the Criminal Procedure Act was passed in
October 2011, yet may not come into force un til October this year. That Act amends
numerous other Acts, including the Chateau  Companies Act 1977. That is fine and
good, one might say, but John Banks came al ong and repealed the Chateau Companies
Act 1977 using the Regulatory Reform (Repeals) Act in August 2012. So the left hand
of National does not appear to know what the right hand of John Banks is doing, and it
is amending a repealed Act. So long comm encement dates are not, in general, a good
idea.
This debate will conclude soon and the Co mmittee will vote. My vote may be cast in
person or it may be cast by proxy, and I ac knowledge and thank the Greens for their
support of democracy. Six other MPs may be in the same position as me, and it is good
that they are able to participate as MPs, the equal of my and th eir 114 other colleagues.
But there is a problem when it comes to vot ing on this bill, which is that we have a
Prime Minister who thinks we should not be  able to vote here. Th e only thing toxic is
that we have a Prime Minister with contem pt for democracy, and that clearly will not
do. The Holidays (Full Recognition of Wa itangi Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment
Bill will pass, despite the Prime Minister’s  toxicity, with the votes of Labour, the
Greens, New Zealand First, the M āori Party, Mana, United Future, and me as an
independent MP. I gladly support this bill.
