years—the next 1 or 2 years. It  is all right talki ng about 10 years’ ti me. It is like the
Labour Party’s superannuation policy. We hear about that in 10 years’ time, but what
we need to know is about the next 2 years. In the next 2 years, what will be the effect of
this bill? I do not know what that effect will be until Mr Clark tells this Committee what
it will be, because I think he understands the issues involved. It may be—

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: Will he tell us?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: No, he will tell us. I have got great faith in Mr Clark, because I
have found him to be an honest individual.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: He won’t duck?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I do not think that he will duck from the question, but I do
think that he is not to use the line that this is  the best legislation in the last 50 years. No,
he cannot use that line with regard to this  legislation, and he ca nnot use the line about
the next 50 years and talk about holidays ove r those years. We want to know about the
next 2 years—just the next 2 years—to just before the next electi on. That is what Mr
Clark should concentrate on, the time before the next election. Will this bill make any
difference? I do not know whether he is going to find that this bill makes any difference
to ordinary New Zealanders in that time. It  would be disappointing if this House was
spending time on a bill, and that member has staged his political career on a bill, that
achieves nothing—a bill that achieves nothing in the next 2 years.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: This member would know a lot about that.
27 Mar 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9009

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Is that what this member is going to talk about? Mr Robertson
there says: “You’d know all abou t that.” Well, I would like to see Mr Robertson come
to Hamilton and campaign. I want to see him come and campaign when we have got a
$2 billion expressway going through our city that is going to be the best thing—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Sorry, Mr Chairman. Mr Robe rtson distracted me for a
moment there, and I would hate to be distracted on a bill like this.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call
in the Committee stage of the Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC
Day) Amendment Bill. David Bennett, the member who has just resumed his seat, has
delusions of grandeur. I think he might thin k he is Simon Crean, or someone like that. I
am not sure whether there is a comparison for Mr Bennett in either the Australian Labor
Party caucus or, indeed, any othe r caucus whatsoever. He is a unique contributor to our
House.
I wanted to pick up just one  of the points that was ma de by Mr Bennett around when
this bill is going to actually make a pract ical difference, and it is quite confusing
listening to National Party members on this bill. It is either a bill that will destroy the
fabric of our society as we know it or a bill that is going to have no impact whatsoever
so why are we bothering, and both arguments  are being run at the moment by the
National Party. In fact, I think David Bennett may even have run both arguments during
that speech—actually, possibly even in the same sentence. So I think we just need to
clarify a few matters for the National Party on that point.
It is true that the next time this bill will have an effect is 2015, so that gives us plenty
of time to get ourselves prep ared for that to occur. The Labour Party in Government in
2015, assisted by others, perhaps, in the House,  will celebrate the fact that when we
come to 2015 this bill will come into force. Then it will have an effect in 2016, and then
in 2021. So Mr Bennett can rest easy in his be d in Hamilton, knowing that this bill will
have an effect in those periods.
The couple of points I just wanted to raise in this call are, firstly, a specific point,
which is around the issue that has been raised from time to time about the cost of this
legislation and the cost of this  legislation to businesses. The reason I want to raise it is
that early on in this debate the Prime Mini ster got himself very exercised and excited
about the potential cost of this bill to businesses, and in the end the figures he was using
sort of fell apart on him and were largely discredited. But I know that the Government is
particularly attracted to the numbers that it gets provided by David Farrar. The numbers
that David Farrar provides to the National Part y are things that they  take seriously, so I
think we should note that he has done the calculation.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: They pay for them.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: They do pay for those numbers—that is right. But the
calculation he has done on this bill is that it would, if pa ssed, add 0.12 percent to the
wage bill of a company—0.12 percent. It is not a massive task.
It is interesting to note in the National Party’s polls that Da vid Farrar actually
supports this bill along with, I suspect, a larg e number of other Na tional Party MPs.
That is the really sad thing today. This H ouse will, I hope, at the end of this Committee
stage pass this bill through, and it will go then to the third reading. That will happen
because a coalition of parties in this Chamber has come together around a sensible idea,
an idea that is not actually—

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: It’s called a motley crew.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: A motley crew, says Louise Upston, channelling her
1980s hair metal band. But, you know, we will not go into the history of hair metal
bands. I would not want to offend the Chair in  that regard, either. What we do know is
9010 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 27 Mar 2013
that the coalition of parties other than the National Party and the ACT Party in this
House is supporting this bill because it is a se nsible bill. It is a bill that says we
recognise the importance of Waitangi Day and Anzac Day to New Zealanders. We say
that those days deserve full recognition.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: Oh!

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Mr Auchinvole is concerned ab out that, but when we look
at Australia the evidence is that attenda nce at Anzac Day ceremonies increased when
this law was put in place in the states that have it, and that is because it provides people
with a focus around the period where it is a we ekend, where they can ensure that they
have their time off.
The other point to note is, of course, that Anzac Day is in fact a holiday during the
week, and people do not suddenly disavow themselves of commemorating people
because it is a holiday during th e week. All this bill does is say that if Anzac Day falls
on a weekend, New Zealanders will get the holidays that they deserve in the Holidays
Act. It is by no means, in any way, an assault on Anzac Day. It is , in fact, a way of
ensuring that New Zealanders can fully co mmemorate two very important days and
have time with their families. It is an excellent bill.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Thank you very much indeed for the
opportunity to speak on this particular bill,  the Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi
Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill, in the name of David Clark. I am put in mind
of that grand Kiwi tradition during festive occasions, sports days, and picnic days—a
good old-fashioned kids’ lolly scramble, because th at is what this bill reminds me of. Is
this really the way, one has to ask, to in troduce oneself as a serious member of
Parliament concerned with legislation for the country’s good? Is it?

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Habeas corpus.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: The Habeas Corpus Amendment Bill is a very serious
piece of legislation. It  is a very serious pi ece of legislation that  was accepted. I will be
interested to see whether this gets the same vote. I agree with my colleague the chair of
the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee, David Bennett, that this is a member
whom we had credited with having really good potential. We thought that this could be
a David with a future in the Labour Party.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. This is the Committee
stage of this bill. I think it would behove the members opposite to at least address the
content of the bill at some point.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Well, the debate has certainly been quite
wide ranging and actually quite humorous, I have to say, from both sides. I am
monitoring it very closely. This is a time-lim ited debate, and if members want to waste
their time in a time-limited debate, that is up to them, but I am keeping track.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: There we go. Savaged by Iain Lees-Galloway—savaged
and almost brought to silence. But let us just go on.
Think of this wrapped in gift paper by your new Labour MP David Clark. I think it is
a pity to embark on a political career in qui te that way. The politici an concerned is, in
my mind, a serious politician—a  serious politician—and I ju st think it does not quite
carry the significance of the day as a comme morative day to declare it a holiday. Anzac
Day is very, very special, and here we go, making it a holiday. Wh at happened to those
sector groups that created picnic days? Do you remember the picnic days? The good old
Auckland picnic days? They did not stay a picnic day for ve ry long. They are just part
of being a day off.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Trade unions.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Trade unions—that is right.  The emphasis changes when
things are declared holidays rather than commemorative days. It was moving to hear
27 Mar 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9011
Simon O’Connor reading from an Anzac diary dur ing the second reading of this bill. It
was moving. And it was disturbing to hear the criticism from the other side of the
Chamber, and here we go again.
The process of this bill—members opposite would like me to talk  about the process
of the bill. I again share the views of Mr Be nnett, the charismatic chair of the Transport
and Industrial Relations Committee—a charismatic chairman. He made some very
gracious remarks towards the way this bill was introduced and the way it was presented,
and I would concur with those, because it wa s well presented. It was spoken to well by
people who came in to make submissions from  both sides. I see a head shaking on the
other side. I am speaking in favour of the pr esentation that we received. You should not
be critical of your own member, but we unders tand that is a little bit of a difficulty for
that particular party over there.
But then again, as my colleague said, wa s it a good presentation, or was it in fact
flimflam? Is this a road to being a David with  a future within the Labour Party? What is
in a name? Well, if the name is David, one is  part of a plethora, a whole clan of them.
But does this differentiate David definitively?
How does the bill compare with Nationa l policies passing through the same
committee? Let us think of what some of  those might be. National introduced the 90-
day trial period for new employees in small and medium sized businesses in 2009. What
would that do, compared with this bill, which gives people holidays? That created
13,000 jobs—13,000 jobs. This committee had anothe r piece of legislation go through,
which members will remember, expanding the 90-day trial to all businesses in 2011.
Research shows the Government’s 90-day trial period is en couraging businesses to take
a chance—

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a ca ll on this bill, the Holidays
(Full Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC  Day) Amendment Bill. I am delighted
to see David Clark, the person whose name it is in, is the member in the chair.
The Greens absolutely support this bill, a nd I take exception to the comments of
Chris Auchinvole, the previous speaker. He sounded so aghast at the thought of workers
actually taking a holiday. It reminded me very much of the Christmas story, the
Christmas tale, and Mr Scrooge. Workers do need holidays. Workers are working
longer hours than they ever have before, and the reason they are doing this is that wages
have been forced lower and lower and lowe r through this Government’s lack of action
around developing proper jobs and a decent standard of living for workers.
If you compare what New Zealanders get in  terms of public holidays and statutory
holidays, we are falling below the OECD countries in terms of generosity for workers to
have time to relax. This bill is a way of addressing that. This bill goes some way
towards saying that workers actually deserve 11 days off—that it is feasible for them to
take their 11 statutory holidays every year, instead of having to be short-changed every
5 years or so when Waitangi Day and Anzac Day fall on a weekend.
We reject the notion that by Mondayis ing both Waitangi Day and Anzac Day it
somehow cheapens their commemoration. Other speakers have noted that this happens
already if 25 December or the day after that day fall on a Sunday, and also if New
Year’s Day or the day after that day fall on a Sunday. All four of these holidays are
transferred, so it does not actu ally cheapen the event. In fa ct, the day itself is the day
that people commemorate. Both Anzac Day a nd Waitangi Day are sacred and they will
remain sacred wherever they fall in the wee k, as has already been noted, as well, by Mr
Grant Robertson from the Labour Party.
If we think about what is coming up this w eekend, it is Easter, a nd Easter is falling
this week at the end of March. Easter neve r ever stays on the same days, because the
timing of that holiday is attached to the moon. In fact, it is a lunar holiday.
9012 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 27 Mar 2013

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: It’s not attached to the moon.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: It is a lunar holiday. However,  the fact that the actual days
change does not cheapen the resurrection and death of Christ.
When this bill Mondayises both Waitang i Day and Anzac Day, it may well increase
participation. Certainly, this has been the example in Australia for Anzac Day. At
Waitangi Day we have seen many, many people turn up on both the day before and the
actual day. When it falls on a weekend ther e is a lower participation rate, because
people cannot attach the extra day to the w eekend. Local businesses up there have said
that when it falls close to the start of a weekend, it actually in creases the amount of
business that they have in their community.
I guess if we are to think about Anzac Day and Waitangi Day as days that we should
commemorate, then we should also think about the fact that we n eed to allow workers
time to celebrate them. Whether it falls on a Sunday, or whether it falls on a Friday, for
that matter, or a Thursday, the fact remains that each of these days is special and
workers do participate in the celebrations and the commemorations around them. It is
not onerous for businesses for th is to be brought to fruition. Th ere is a 2-year run-in for
them to plan for it, and other speakers have already told you about the minimal cost that
it will bring for small businesses.
This—[Interruption] I was just having a small holiday there. This bill is supported.
This bill is definitely supported—

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: On behalf of New Zealand First I would like to
take a brief call on this very important bi ll, the Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi
Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill. This bill is really important. We know that
Anzac Day and Waitangi Day are days that are really significant to us as New
Zealanders and we will not stop commemorati ng them. They are very, very special and
we always like to treat those days as such. But what we in New Zealand First believe is
that the rules for these holidays have to be the same as they are for Christmas and New
Year if they fall on a Saturday or a Sunday. It is absolutely essential. We want to
recognise our special days. We do not want them being trea ted as second-rate holidays,
and we believe that this is happening at th is point in time. So we are happy for this
particular bill to go through.
It was interesting to hear that the tourism industry ab solutely supports  this bill
because it knows that people will travel further into New Zealand if there is a day off on
the Monday when the Saturday or the Sunday is Waitangi Day or Anzac Day. I have
had a lot of people saying to me—even the taxi driver when I came into Parliament this
particular week said that he thinks we  should have the Monday off when it is a
significant holiday. People suppo rt this change right th roughout New Zealand. But I
think it is worth saying that 6 February and 25 April are still going to remain as the days
that we commemorate and observe Anzac Day and Waitangi Day. What this bill means
is that if these days fall on the weekend, then a holiday on the Monday can be observed.
The importance and the recognition of these da ys is absolutely essential. We like to
compare ourselves with Australia. Australia  has implemented this Mondayisation very
successfully and, as New Zealanders, we can  do the same. They are the people whom
we like to measure ourselves against all the time. Even the Prime Minister measures us
against that country.
We were quite interested to hear that the fi rst date that will actually be affected by
this change is in April 2015—25 April. I think it is worth me ntioning that this is the
100-year anniversary of Gallipoli, and what be tter way to celebrate. It is very, very
important. The first time that this affects Wa itangi Day is in February 2016. So we can
see that it is not going to happen instantly, but it is going to happen over a period of
time. I think it will affect us for 2 days every 5 years, which is not significant.
27 Mar 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9013
What is the cost to employers? Well, we have heard that it is going to be only 0.12
percent. This is not going to put an undue  financial burden on the Government or on
taxpayers, mainly because it is going to happen only occasionally. In New Zealand First
we like to see some consistency across our public holidays. The in consistency that we
currently have is quite problematic and it can be quite confusing for families,
employers, and employees alike. So we need to ensure that all public holidays are
treated the same.
It is worth stating too that this bill is  going to be excellent for provincial New
Zealand and those in the touris m sector. It is time that we stood up for this group in this
Chamber. The cycleways—the great tourism development—do not appeal to a large
majority of the population, because we are ne ver ever going to use them, but in some
way this small change, by Mondayising Anzac  Day and Waitangi Da y, will inevitably
benefit families, communities, and many businesses right throughout New Zealand. It is
for this reason that New Zealand First is firmly in support of this bill.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I am pleased to support the Committee stage of the
Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi Da y and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill. I
wanted to start by saying a c ouple of things—first  of all, to the chair of the Transport
and Industrial Relations Committee, Davi d Bennett, who talked at length about
disappointment. Actually, I think if anyone deserves sympathy when it comes to
disappointment, it is that member, who has been in this House for several years now and
must be feeling very disappointed about th e way his Government is treating him. In
fact, we say “David Bennett for Minister”.  And we would vote fo r you, David, if we
had the chance. And then to Mr Chri s Auchinvole, who al so talked about
disappointment, I have got tw o words to say to that me mber, the two words being
“habeas corpus”. If we have ever had so significant a member’s bill passed in this
House, it was today with the Habeas Corpus Amendment Bill, as we heard earlier.
I wanted to point out to the members opposite that on Anzac Day and Waitangi Day,
every year apart from every 5 years there is actually a holiday. It is a public holiday. So
what happens is that people get the day off. Some of them—many of them, these days—
go off to the Anzac Day ceremonies in the mo rning, the commemorations first thing in
the morning. Some people on Waitangi Day go off to celebrate Waitangi Day. Some
people do not, but it is a holiday. So this idea that somehow, because this bill gives
people a holiday once every 5 or 7 years, it is cheapening those days is, quite frankly,
ridiculous.
I also wanted to respond to the memb er Simon O’Connor, who spent his 10
minutes—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Who?

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: —Simon O’Connor—in the second reading of this bill reading
out the diary of a Gallipoli soldier who did not come home. I have to say, Mr O’Connor,
that I found that incredibly offensive. I thought it was us ing the deaths of working-class
men like my grandfather who went to the wa r. I say to Mr O’Connor to have a look
above the next time he comes out of the National Party caucus room at the shield for the
Peter Fraser Government, and he will see a photo of my grandfather, who fought in the
First World War, who came home, and who joined the Labour Party—who joined the
Labour Party—to fight for justice for work ing people. I know he would not begrudge
the provisions in this bill. He would not. I thought it really cheapened the memory of
the people in my family and the people in everyone’s families to have done that. I
thought that was disgraceful.
The other thing that has been very interesting in this debate is that the Government
seems to have forgotten its own legisla tion. In 2010 it passed legislation that would
enable public holidays to be transferred to another day, including Waitangi Day and
9014 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 27 Mar 2013
Anzac Day—including those precious days. But in 2010 the Government did not think
they were precious enough to stop them from be ing transferred. In fact, in its legislation
introducing the Holidays Amendment Bill to the House, the bill talked about it. An
example it gave in the explanatory note said : “For example, if Wa itangi Day falls on a
Wednesday, an employer and a group of employees who work Monday to Friday may
agree to observe Waitangi Day on the Friday.”  So what happened to the preciousness of
Waitangi Day? Another example used in the bill was Anzac Day. This Government
cannot have it both ways. It cannot stand up in  this Chamber and say this is all about
disrespecting the memory of Gallipoli and the people who have gone before us who
fought for freedom and democracy, and at the same time forget that it has passed
legislation that actually undermines the recognition of those important days and, in fact,
makes it more difficult for many workers to actually have the day off on pay.
I just want to finish, if I may, with a very interesting quote that we heard in

items.speaker: Parliament today. This comes from our Prime Minister
items.text: “Mondayisation, I know, I don’t
agree with that. I mean, I think in the end this is an issue which, you know, fair enough,
I don’t think, you know, our—we’re opposed, but we’re not vehemently opposed.” That
was the Prime Minister of New Zealand, John Key, who cannot make up his mind, who
instructed the chair of the Transport an d Industrial Relations Committee to oppose it.
And that is why those members have, because they have no basis for that.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: I would like to acknowledge Dr David Clark for
having a member’s bill before Parliament . It is well done. Anzac Day, 25 April—25

items.speaker: April
items.text: a day of respect, a day of commemoration, a day of reflection, a day of
significance, and a unique day that marks the sacrifice of generati on after generation.
Allow me to paint a picture for you. The place is Pukekura Park, New Plymouth. A
young boy, 3 or 4 years old; the first time he had heard a band with the kettle drums; the
first time, probably, he had heard a pipe band and felt that curious tingling at the back of
the neck that anybody w ith antecedents from Scotland al ways feels when they hear the
pipes; long lines of men and some women snaking into the ground;  at the back the
school cadets; and before them—it is shortly after the Korean War—quite a few Korean
War veterans, the larger majority of Worl d War II veterans, and a smaller number of
World War I veterans. But the smallest gr oup—the smallest group; very, very small—
probably fewer than a dozen frail older me n, with their medals clacking, the poppies on
their chest, was walking at the head of the parade into Pukekura Park in New Plymouth.
Among those men was my grandfather Haro ld Morley Thompson. These were the
men, the last men, a few of the New Zeal and Mounted Rifles who had gone to South
Africa to serve in New Zealand’s first overseas campaign. Almost 6,500 New
Zealanders served in that campaign. I guess th at was the first time I felt that sense of
pride in the fact that my gr andad was there. And, sitting on  his knee and listening to his
stories of that campaign, I became aware of  what it meant to serve King—or at that
stage Queen—and country. I remember him be ing enormously proud. I remember him
being enormously proud to be part of it , to be there on Anzac Day, and I remember
hearing some of the stories. If I could be indulged by the Committee, I remember him
telling a story that somehow he committe d the unwritten crime—well, it is not
unwritten; it is quite clearl y written down—of not having th e rifle that you have been
issued with. He was a mounted rifleman  but had no rifle—he had a carbine.
Unfortunately, the carbine has a much shorte r range than a rifle. He was engaging the
Boer at some 500 yards. His commanding officer heard the crack as Thompson engaged
the enemy, and recognised that it was not a rifle—he recognised that it was a carbine—
and said “Thompson, 200 yards forward.” He su rvived that unfortuna te brush with the
increased proximity of the enemy, and lived to come back to New Zealand and have a
very long and successful life.
27 Mar 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9015
Some years later I was leading my own platoon of school cadets in the Anzac parade
in the same place at Pukekura Park and I vent ure to suggest that all the students—even
though we were all young, at 13, 14, 15, and 16—on th at parade were very cognisant of
the sacrifices made on their behalf by those who were not there with them on that Anzac
Day parade. A few years later, as a member  of the Otago University Medical Company,
“the Blue Berets”, I attended many a Dawn Parade in Dunedin, met the veterans, heard
their stories, and was introduced to the notorious Dawn Parade rum coffee.
More recently I have been honoured to at tend the Dawn Service at the Manurewa
Cenotaph. I see a colleague across the Chamber from me today whom I remember being
there a couple of years ago. The colleague I have just mentioned and another colleague
from the Labour Party had arrived without a wreath, so, in the spirit of the day, I
gestured to them to come up, and we laid the wreath together as local MPs in the area. It
was an indication of the special, unique nature of the day. I just want to leave—

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: I am tempted to
respond to some of the sillier things that National members ha ve offered in this debate
this afternoon, but I do not want to wast e my time on that, except to say to David
Bennett that if he thinks that I am the Si mon Crean of the New Zealand Labour Party,
then I call him the Ken Wyatt of the New Zealand National Party.
The wafer-thin arguments that we have h eard from National members this afternoon
against this bill, the Holidays (Full R ecognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day)
Amendment Bill, represent the very poor opini on that National members of Parliament
have of the people of New Zealand. For some reason, those members of Parliament
think that New Zealanders, given the opportunity of a long weekend when Anzac Day is
commemorated on a Saturday or a Sunday, will  all charge off to the beach and forget
the solemn respect they have for the day, the people, and the sacrifice that they made.
That was the argument that Mike Sabin made, that all of a sudden—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: That’s right.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: “That’s right.”, he says. He  has so little confidence in
New Zealanders that he believes that, give n half an opportunity, they will walk away
from Anzac Day. Well, ladies and gentlemen, people who are listenin g to this debate
and watching this debate, mark that. That  is what Mike Sabin and the National
Government think of you. That is what he th inks of New Zealanders, that they have so
little respect for Anzac Day, for our armed for ces, for our veterans, and for the sacrifice
that they made for our freedom that they wi ll walk away from Anzac Day if they have a
long weekend.
Well, I have experienced a perfect example of how people can easily deal with this.
Anzac Day commemorations are held up and do wn this country. If families choose to
do that outrageous thing of spending a few days away together, they can go to an Anzac
service in the place where they go on holiday. How hard is that—how hard is that?
Communities up and down New Zealand, larg e and small, all commemorate Anzac
Day, and if people are away from home , they can simply go to the Anzac Day
commemoration in the part of the country they go to.
I did this when I was a stude nt association president. We  had university games held
on the weekend that Anzac Day fell on, and a ll the student association presidents
realised that it was important for us to go and respect and acknowledge the day in the
place where we were at. It was very easy to organise and it was very easy to do.
The second ridiculous argument that the National Government has proposed is that
this will cost businesses more than they can  afford. Well, as David Farrar pointed out,
this will cost businesses around 0.1 percent of their wage bi ll. That is how much their
wage bill is going to increase by—0.1 percent. That  is not of their total turnover; it is of
their wage bill. Well, if National has done  so much damage to the New Zealand
9016 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 27 Mar 2013
economy that a 0.1 percent increase to their wage bill will put businesses under, then
that is a sad indictment on this Government’s failure in economic management.
Thirdly, there is the argument  that this bill will have no effect until 2015. Well, that,
again, sums up the National approach to po litics—that if it does not do something

politics and results before the next electi on, and it has no long-term plan for this

The arguments we have heard, and the hiding behind the stories of the
commemoration of Anzac Day, of the sacrifices made at Gallipoli, at Passchendaele, at

SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): It is a pleasure to rise and talk to this
bill, the Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment
Bill. I want to acknowledge the member Davi d Clark for the work that he has done on
this bill and, although I disagree with the bill in premise, the dignity that he has brought
to the approach.
Unfortunately, though, I have found the accusations—thos e hecklings and
interjections a week or so ago—disturbing, and even more so today. Once again it has
been brought up in this place about raising the topic of Anzac Day, bringing up the
story, without comment—that is really important—unlike other members today who
have tried to put words into the mouths of the war dead. I stood up, I only read a war
diary, and I allowed those words to speak fo r themselves. The howls and the cries! I
repeat what I said that day: how dare members opposite act with contempt when the
words of the war dead are spoken—the wo rds of an Anzac trooper are spoken—when
we are discussing Anzac Day. You do not have to  agree with it. You can interpret it in
whatever way you want. It was left free—it was left free. But to rage and rant about
someone daring to talk about Anzac Day—if someone dares to talk about Anzac Day
and to put a bill down, we might put it in context. We might put it in context.
I have been struck since that speech by th e number of phone calls, emails, and letters
that people have sent expr essing their support for that  position, expressing support for
their own people—war veterans, like a member who spoke earlier, who also had people
who served. They were proud as Kiwis to have the voice of an Anzac trooper spoken in
this Chamber. It might pay for members to note, of course, that this Chamber is a war
memorial. In this very Chamber of a war me morial, they have yelled and cajoled the
very fact that we might talk about Anzac Day when discussing a bill about Anzac Day.
That is very, very striking.
I noted a week ago, and I want to note it again today, that Anzac Day is not a
holiday, and that Anzac Day is not an excuse for a holiday. I made it clear the other time
and I want to do so again. If we want to talk  about more holidays, if we want to talk
about workers’ rights, then we can find an  opportunity to do that and discuss it. The
moment you take a day of co mmemoration and turn it into a holiday, you have changed
the nature of the day. That is why we ca ll something a commemoration and that is why
we call something else a holiday.

items.speaker: We have heard from Opposition members who say
items.text: “Oh, this is the same as Easter.
This is the same as Christmas.” That is  just ignorance. Those are days that are

holidays—holy days—days of festival and celebration. Anzac Day is not; it is a day of

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: So Boxing Day’s a holy day? Tau Henare might think that.
SIMON O’CONNOR: We do that in that way. We can see that Mr Mallard is back
in the Chamber. We celebrate different da ys in different ways, and, once again, this
Parliament does a disservice  by trying to make everything absolutely the same. We

But there are a couple of ot her things that we need to  point to. There have been

Attendances over the years have dropped off in some generations in some cities
represented in this House— certainly not in mine. Younge r people and my generation
are coming back to Anzac Day, and that is an important distinction.
So I want to return to what has been a theme of my approach to this bill: that Anzac

of the 25 th. It is a day of commemoration for which Parliament can stand up with

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: I would just like to make a final contribution on this
bill, the Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment
Bill, and just repeat that Anzac Day is a day of respect, a day of commemoration—

items.speaker: Barbara Stewart
items.text: It always is.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: —a day of reflection—I agree—a nd a day of significance. It is
actually unique. It marks the sacrifices of generation after generation. It is a special day.
If Anzac Day falls on a weekend and there is no extra holiday, then so be it—so be it. If
anything, that underscores the extremely special nature of that day. In fact, if you think
about it, it is a very small price to pay—a  small price to pay—for New Zealanders of
today, given the ultimate sacrifice made by the servicemen and servicewomen of
yesterday. I oppose this bill.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I take a call on the Ho lidays (Full Recognition
of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment B ill. I was not intending to take a call,
but I will, having heard some of the comm ents of the National Party members on the
other side. I take a call in response to th e previous speaker, Simon O’Connor, as I am
one of the very few members in this House w ho can say: “I lost my brother in the Viet
Nam War.” I am absolutely appalled at the comments that were made by that member in
relation to that. I have got every right to speak  in this Chamber when I have lost a very
loving, dear one myself, in terms of him falling on behalf of this country.
What I can say, further to some of the commen ts made in this Chamber, is that there
are people who travel around this  country to go to Anzac Da y services and to be with
their families, who have lost people, and go and see the very memorials of their own
9018 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 27 Mar 2013
loved ones. In my particular situation, my loved one has his memorial in Waipukurau in
Hawke’s Bay. I happen to live in Auckland. I would very much like, perhaps on a long
weekend, to be able to travel down to Waipukurau in Hawke’s Bay, spend the weekend

his old friends in Waipukurau, but you cannot do that if Anzac Day falls, for instance,

But I can tell you that the next  time there is a l ong weekend I would dearly love to be

Likewise, around New Zealand I am sure  there are many elderly people—many
elderly people—who would enjoy having their family visit from afar. So many people

an Anzac weekend, a long weekend, to be able to say: “We will go home and visit mum

with them and spend a long weekend with th em.” I certainly know that my sons and
daughters would love to do that with th eir grandparents who are living in Taup ō. They
would love the opportunity to go down a nd spend an Anzac Day weekend down there
and take in Anzac Day in Taupō.
I have heard so much drivel from this National Party that it is unbelievable. A few
years ago I was in Australia with my wife , and we happened to be there on a weekend
when Anzac Day was being celebrated. We were in Sydney and we were absolutely
astounded by the turnout in Sydney. The para de went on for something like 4 hours in
Sydney, around the central city streets. Hundr eds of thousands of people were watching
the parade, and it was a wonderful long w eekend—and not only tha t; the Australians
celebrated as well. It was not just a sad o ccasion; it was also a celebration of their
nation, remembering the Anzacs, remembering those who had fallen but also
celebrating their lives.
Over that weekend there was a lot of celeb ration and also remembering what those
young men and women had done in the name of their country. I think the people on the
Government benches just need to absolutely  wake up and think abou t this for a change.
They should think about humanity for a cha nge, think about the people of New Zealand
for a change, and stop being like lemmings bei ng led over the cliff by their leader, John
Key. They should stop being taken down a road  because they have all been whipped
into action and told what to say. Have some thought for yourselves, have a mind of your
own, think for yourselves, and think of what your const ituents are saying. And your
constituents, Mr Bennett, in Hamilton—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! You are bringing me into the
debate.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: David Bennett should ask the people in Hamilton what
they think. The previous speaker, Mr O’ Connor, should ask the constituents in T āmaki
what they think. I do not think the members ha ve asked their constituents, because most

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I am not quite sure what the previous
speaker, Andrew Williams, was going on about. If he could possibly send me a text at 2
o’clock in the morning, I will take time to  look over it. Coming back to the Holidays
(Full Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill, I just want to

27 Mar 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9019
the Transport and Industrial Relations Co mmittee, I also acknowledge the select

I actually believe that members across the Chamber—certainly the Labour Party—

We go on. Another former MP, one Mr Mars hall, said: “I belie ve that it would

We go on. There are actually other conseq uences to this bill, and those are

I just want, lastly, to refl ect on those veterans who have  served this country. We
